newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq warns Turkey over cordon, US over no-fly zones.
newsitem.headline: Iraq warns Turkey over cordon, US over no-fly zones.

text.p: Iraq warned its northern neighbour Turkey on Sunday not to go ahead with plans to set up a security zone inside Kurdish-held territory in northern Iraq.

"We will take every necessary action in our part to prevent it (the buffer zone)," said Hamed Youssef Hummadi, head of the culture and information committee of Iraq's parliament. He did not elaborate on what measures Iraq might take.

It was Baghdad's first warning to its northern neighbour since Ankara started a military build-up along their common border in an apparent attempt to establish a 5-10 km (three to six mile) -wide cordon to deter attacks by rebel Turkish Kurds.
Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Saturday that Turkey might empty some settlements within the buffer zone.

Turkey fears that rebels of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), fighting for self-rule in southeast Turkey using bases in northern Iraq, will profit from the inter-Kurdish fighting there to mount attacks across the moutainous and porous border.
The United States fired 44 cruise missiles at Iraqi military targets last week and widened a no-fly zone in the south in response to Iraq's incursion into the Kurdish-held north at the end of August.

Turkey's buffer zone, if established, would be within territory under the control of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which has allied itself with Iraq against its old rival, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
Lightly-armed KDP guerrillas and tank-equipped divisions from Iraq's elite force of Republican Guards jointly seized control of the main Kurdish stronghold of Arbil from the PUK on August 31.
Iraq, keen to resume some form of trade with Turkey despite U.N. trade sanctions imposed on Baghdad for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, has always been cautious not to antagonise its northern neighbour.
"Iraq is now engaged in two main fronts - the row with U.S. over its air-umbrellas and struggle to win minds and hearts of its ethnic Kurds," said another diplomat.

Iraq's official media denied that Iraqi troops were arresting and killing ethnic Turks, known as Turkomans, in Arbil but made no reference to Ciller who made the accusation after a meeting with the U.S. ambassador in Turkey on Saturday.
Iraqi media on Sunday also reiterated Baghdad's threats to shoot down U.S. or allied aircraft flying over Iraq.

The official newspapers Jumhouriya, Thawra and Qadissiya all carried on their front pages a foreign ministry statement vowing that "our air defences throughout Iraq will hit at any hostile target violating our skies."
Iraq's military said on Saturday it had fired surface-to-air missiles but they had missed. The Pentagon said it could not confirm that missiles had been fired at U.S. planes.
"Now we have announced that their areas (no-fly zones) are null and void and we will take every opportunity to shoot down U.S. planes in the whole areas," Hummadi said.
